questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,0,8)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+4y+x$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-2,0,8)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,0)} & =(-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+4(0)+(-2) \\  & =-2-2 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-2,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,0)}(y-0) \\ z-8 & =-4(y-0) \\ z & =-4y+8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,0,8)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=-4y+8\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{{e}^{x}-{e}^{y}}{2x}+2y$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(1,1,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,1).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,1) & =\frac{{e}^{1}-{e}^{1}}{2(1)}+2(1) \\  & =0+2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},0,2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{2}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2} \\  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot 1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-\frac{\pi }{2},0) & ={f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0)(y-0) \\ z-2 & =-\frac{1}{2}y \\ z & =-\frac{1}{2}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},0,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=-\frac{1}{2}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-\frac{1}{2}y+2$ (or $y+2z-4=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,2⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,2⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-2j+k \\  & =⟨0,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,-2,1⟩.$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Given that the point $P(4,-2,5)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=y\sqrt{x}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(4,-2,5)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(4,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)} & =(-2)\sqrt{4} \\  & =-2(2) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(4,-2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)}(x-4) \\ z-5 & =-4(x-4) \\ z & =-4x+21\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,-2,5)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=-2 \\ z=-4x+21\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$
